rv.q: It is richly steeped in Irish folkloric tradition and philosophical enquiry emphasised by designer Rae Smith’s diaphanous screens that partition the set at various intervals.

But before that is what the real McPherson heads have been waiting for: The Brightening Air, his first original play since The Night Alive in 2013. It’s a slow, wistful start, the dial firmly tuned to ‘Chekhov’. The setting is a semi-dilapidated County Sligo farmhouse, at some point in the ‘80s.

Conor McPherson’s great plays creep up on you. There are the ghost stories that lead somewhere emotionally devastating in The Weir. There are the tales from a 1930s boarding house that can reduce you to rubble when mixed with Bob Dylan songs in Girl from the North Country (back here at the Old Vic in London once this new show ends).
Setting the table with sandwiches is Dermot’s estranged wife Lydia (Hannah Morrish), desperately in love with him and pleading for some magical water that will make him love her back.
